question: On 28 May 2026, the pharmaceuticals company Sandoz lodged an anti-dumping complaint concerning Chinese imports of 6-aminopenicillanic acid, a key ingredient in the production of amoxicillin, the world’s most widely used antibiotic1. Commissioner Ribera has stated that: ‘The Critical Medicines Act is about improving a secure supply of vital medicines in Europe.

’2 With the trilogue agreement expected to be adopted shortly, we call on the Commission to act without delay to protect our amoxicillin producers from Chinese competition. The Commission’s respect for confidentiality obligations from the moment the complaint is received, even before any investigation may be opened is laudable. 1.

Could the Commission nevertheless confirm and publish the studies or reports carried out by its services on Chinese commercial practices in the medicines sector, and more specifically regarding antibiotics, as well as on the situation in the amoxicillin supply chain (including components thereof) and the anticipated risks of supply disruptions?

What approach does it intend to take to address the increasing number of requests for investigations from European companies across all sectors, in order to ensure swifter processing and a more effective defence against unfair practices? Does it intend to review the current timetable?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.9.2026) The trade defence investigations are fact-based and the Commission’s findings are disclosed and become publicly available at provisional and definitive stage in the Official Journal.

More broadly, the new Pharmaceutical Regulation1, on which co-legislators found a political agreement in December 2025, will provide a robust EU framework for managing critical shortages and identify vulnerabilities in the supply chain of critical medicines, including of dependencies on third countries for their manufacturing.

This new regulatory framework will be complemented by the Critical Medicines Act2 which aims to address upstream supply chain vulnerabilities and offer additional tools to enhance supply security of critical medicines.

To meet the demand for trade defence action, the Commission has opened record numbers of new investigations starting in 2024 and is committed to acting against the injurious effects of unfairly traded imports as quickly as possible.
The Office of Complaints3 of the trade defence services engage with complainants to advise about the information necessary to ensure that draft complaints meet the requisite standards for initiation.

Affected industries need to act fast and be properly prepared when presenting draft complaints to the Directorate-General for Trade and Economic Security (DG TRADE) for assessment to help eliminate delays in the process. The Commission recognises the pivotal role of this sector for the EU and is confident that the recent decision to increase the resources in DG TRADE will have a positive impact.
1 Final compromise text of the Directive: https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-6367-2026-

INIT/en/pdf and the Regulation: https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-6366-2026-INIT/en/pdf. 2 The Critical Medicines Act text on which the EU Council and Parliament reached a provisional agreement in May 2026 available on the Council website at the following link: https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-11059-2026-INIT/en/pdf. 3 https://policy.trade.ec.europa.eu/contacts/trade-defence-enquiries_en.
